And that once you start switching this way, you will see that every project can be seen as a product discovery sprint because everything has uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: We are just in that kind of a space. So that's my short pitch. I've talked about this at length with the product team. I'll probably link at some point to the recorded video. Where I shared this with the product team, and that's a blog post on the topic, and then I'll move on. Jacob, do you want to have any comments?

utterances.speaker: L
utterances.text: No, I mean, this is such a huge— this is an enormous topic that there's no way I could possibly— this has got to be outside of this. But I was just saying that

utterances.speaker: L
utterances.text: sometimes when you can—

utterances.speaker: L
utterances.text: we learned a lot from the repo editor, which was just, I think, one of the bigger things that we worked on, which wound up with like 800 comments. And doing that, just kind of going for it without a fully specced out thing,

utterances.speaker: L
utterances.text: I think we wound up losing a lot of time with that. But we gained a lot of knowledge, but we lost a lot. I don't know. It's a balance. I have to probably see it in action, and maybe we can practice it and get that. But what I was saying is that maybe like when you're painting, you paint the whole picture at once. If you can like lightly sketch out and lightly engineer the whole thing, it doesn't have to be perfect to get it kind of functioning, then you can get some feedback early versus like going hardcore into the details and making everything perfect only to change it.

utterances.speaker: L
utterances.text: Yeah, so that's it. Next person.

utterances.speaker: J
utterances.text: I just want to ask a question to Mark. I know it's a huge topic, so I don't want to start, you know, like a huge humongous discussion, but I'm curious, we have 3 weeks to do something in one release, right? Maybe not even 3 weeks to do that. How do we— it feels to me from the engineering side that there is this huge pressure and expectation that we ship something.

utterances.speaker: J
utterances.text: If something doesn't get shipped, we are very much public, which means everyone gets hammered down from the community, from customers. Disappointment, public disappointment is very big. So it, from my side, that looks like a huge pressure for anyone going into the work when you don't have anything, like even like the light skeleton set, um, and when you're kind of stumbling and, and trying to figure things out.

utterances.speaker: J
utterances.text: So that's, I'm not sure whether that product discovery works in, in our time constraint.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: Well, let me just put it this way. In the teams I'm used to, we would start a sprint, and a sprint was 1 week. We would have zero designs. We would do everything and ship 5 iterations in 1 week. And at the end, it was beautiful, perfectly polished, fully functional. And then maybe at most there's a couple of bugs you'd come up with the following week.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: So by my reckoning, we should be able to do 3 or 4 of these within a release. So our time pressure, I'd say it's the opposite. The time pressure of a month is not a problem, except it's a problem that we're going too slow. We should be able to iterate so much faster than what we're doing today.

utterances.speaker: J
utterances.text: What does that mean, like through the whole stack or just like a feature?

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: Whole stack. No, no, whole stack. End to end delivered.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Awesome. We should do that.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: So in particular, by Wednesday we'd have a design, you know, we'd have the first iteration and it kind of looks ugly. By Wednesday afternoon, we'd have it looking a little bit better. By Thursday it'd be polished more. We'd have metrics in there so that we'd

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: we'd actually have it out to beta customers by Thursday afternoon, and then we'd have monitoring so we'd know if the feature was actually successful or not, so that Friday we could report on it and say, yes, we delivered it, here's what it looks like, and it's validated that this solution actually worked. One week.

utterances.speaker: L
utterances.text: What I currently see is a lot of— so in order for that to work, I think what we'd have to do is we'd have to get the design and be like, that's the design, that's it. But right now there's like a lot of back and forth.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: No, no, no, absolutely not. That is— throw out the design that way. You don't do it that way. What you do is you come up with the tiniest little

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: thing first with the cheapest, ugliest design you possibly can. You ship that, and then you iterate on it, and you improve it, and improve it, and improve it, but you do the small iterations 5 times within 1 week. So you don't absolutely— unequivocally do not start with the full design ahead of time. That would be the wrong direction to go.

utterances.speaker: L
utterances.text: Sounds like the most amount of work for the front-end engineers to me.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: It's not about a total amount of work, it's just about coordination. The real challenge is that you need an overlap of 3 or 4 hours a day with everybody— product design, engineering, frontend, backend. I mean, it's hard in our remote

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: timezone world. So that's why I haven't been pushing this hard, because I don't want to disturb things. But all I can say is, in certain circumstances, it works absolutely beautifully.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: And we should figure out some way to make it work here.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: I think the main problem we're seeing in this topic is that we often— have a decision from product and then we design some mockups and then the product change and then we design other mockups and then the product change again. And this is super hard to, at least on the end, the MVP on that issue, on the issues, uh, they often change and it's hard for the developers to get something done, you know, with a lot of these iterations.

utterances.speaker: D
utterances.text: But also the, the other problem with our velocity. We kind of see our velocity as very big, but like if you look at the minimal time in order to ship even the smallest change, when this smallest change actually lands something very useful, it's right now, I don't know, 3, 4 days basically before it gets reviewed, before someone approves that, before we have the pipeline green, before this lands on dev, before, before anything else.

utterances.speaker: D
utterances.text: So It seems that it's kind of impossible for us to work today at this pace with the process that we have today. So we have to fix our process to be more agile in the way how we can— how quickly we can make change and how quickly we can test this change. Because today this process is only taking longer and longer, something that I believe everyone sees.

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: Just to give a small thing into reviewing merge requests,

utterances.speaker: B
utterances.text: In the most ideal sense, I mostly— it cost me 10 minutes, but often it costs around 30 minutes to get the JDK running and like check out the merge request and like review it properly, find it within the JDK where the changes, etc., etc.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: Like this thing can all be solved with Review Apps, but it is not here yet for GitLab itself.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Maybe one of the other possible improvements, maybe it's already there, but I'm not really sure about that. I see sometimes engineering working on the same person working maybe on two different items, two different issues at the same time. That is good in order to spot possible problems in advance, but it's also hard since then we tend to have merge request merged by the 7th or so.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: And so it is maybe too late to fix or to add or to change at that point. Focusing on one thing at a time. So the whole team or 3 persons at the same time to one specific issue, deliver it sort of early feature freeze just for that issue, and then move on to another one can be useful to avoid the after-feature freeze time that we often need, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Okay, so it seems that the next point is mine too. Always in the same bucket but from a different angle. I feel that sometimes we need to make the team more aware of which is the vision behind the feature, which is the value that we want to deliver.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: To our users. It is not— I'm looking at your comments— yeah, there's nothing else. It's something like having

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: the, say, the value of what we are doing, a part of feeling it our own value. So putting our own experience, our own

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: goals into the specific feature. I don't want to say that people are working on features like robots, absolutely. But sometimes I'd like to see more involvement and to make people aware of what is really important.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: In this case, AutoDevOps, for example, we fought a lot on AutoDevOps. To get it done. And eventually we did it, but I'm not so sure that it was clear that it is a specific case. It was a very important item that really want to be the best MVP, at least the best MVP, that is not the best feature, best MVP for our users.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: So this time we added this process because of a reason. It's not just done a priori. And that is something that we can improve in order to understand what is really important to ship and what is not.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Filippa, you're next.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: My point is to respect UX decisions a little bit more. This, I often feel this on the CI/CD team, and I think we can improve this. I think the feeling is that we can all decide on UX, which I don't think it's the process. If we have a UX team, it's because we need someone expert in UX, and product and engineering teams are not experts on UX.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: So I think we should respect their decisions a little bit more. We can improve on that.

utterances.speaker: H
utterances.text: If there's no other points, not sure if someone wants to add something, or we can end the meeting.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: I just want to say a word about this. Yeah, sometimes I feel that it may happen, may appear that this is the fact. Actually, we as a product, me personally, we are pushing things also to UX in order to make it really clear which is the goal that we want to achieve, which is the value that we want to deliver.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: But frankly, I'm seeing that normally we are at least finding a middle way with UX that is shared, that is agreed. So as far as I know, there is nothing that is shipped or delivered without UX approval, even if sometimes maybe UX is just moving in a different direction and we try to make our point in order to make them understand.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: But it's not a question of taking over UX is a matter of communicating the real value of that. So if it's not clear, I agree that we should improve, not maybe the respect that I see that the respect is there, but at least the communication and this process too.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: So good to know that it could be a problem. We will address it.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Job, do you want to close the meeting? Sure, Fabio.

utterances.speaker: D
utterances.text: This was a good meeting.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: We wanted to be more actionable, we want to be more iterative and more communicative. Well, I think that's a pretty good conclusion to all of it. And I think everyone would agree that if we improve all of those, we'd be even more great. So everyone have a nice day, have a nice week, and see you in a month.

utterances.speaker: E
utterances.text: Goodbye.

chapters.title: Release wins and highlights
chapters.gist: The team celebrates shipping group issue boards, Auto DevOps, and protected runners for the 10.0 release.

chapters.title: Deployment delays and project renaming
chapters.gist: Technical conflicts during the CE to EE merge and confusion over the GitLab Runner rename caused some initial release friction.

chapters.title: Blocked features and missed goals
chapters.gist: The lock issue, GraphQL API, and Postgres high availability did not make the release due to technical and licensing challenges.

chapters.title: Auto DevOps process challenges
chapters.gist: Speakers discuss how late UX involvement and changing requirements made the Auto DevOps launch a rough road for the team.

chapters.title: Improving the retrospective format
chapters.gist: The team debates how to make the retrospective meetings more interactive and focused on actionable process improvements.

chapters.title: Adopting product discovery for speed
chapters.gist: Mark suggests using smaller iterations and early collaborative discovery to ship features significantly faster.

chapters.title: Respecting design and UX decisions
chapters.gist: The meeting concludes with a discussion on better communication and respecting the expertise of the UX team.

action_items.text: Remove the old GitLab CI/Multi-Runner project to restore broken redirects.
Create a clear deprecation process for GitLab applications.
Bring discipline and focus to the retrospective process and track improvements.
Experiment with making smaller merge requests to reduce integration problems.
Involve UX and engineering earlier in the planning process.

content.tldr: The meeting reviewed the successes and failures of the GitLab 10.0 release while debating how to improve internal processes. While the release included major features like Auto DevOps, it was hindered by coordination issues and late involvement of key teams.

bullets.text: Review the results and process of the GitLab 10.0 release.
Group issue boards and Auto DevOps were successfully shipped despite heavy coordination needs.
The retrospective format needs more discussion and fewer pre-written scripts.
The release process suffered from late UX and frontend involvement.
Technical delays in the deployment cycle due to merge conflicts.
Licensing issues that put the GraphQL API project on ice.
The proposed adoption of 'product discovery' to increase shipping speed.
Eric will take responsibility for improving the retrospective and process discipline.
Teams will explore earlier collaboration between product, UX, and engineering.

content.tldr: GitLab 10.0 delivered major functionality but highlighted significant technical debt in the release process. Moving forward, the team aims to fix the deprecation process and improve deployment stability.

bullets.text: Shipped group issue boards and protected runners.
Successfully launched Auto DevOps after a massive team effort.
Merge conflicts between CE and EE delayed the release candidate.
Uncertain licensing and patent issues blocked the GraphQL endpoint.
Postgres high availability was blocked by testing difficulties and broken instances.
Decided to remove the runner project to fix link redirects.
Reverted some deprecations to avoid breaking customer instances.
Fix the background job process to allow merging on release days.
Resolve the lock issue for the 10.1 release.

content.tldr: The team has finished the major 10.0 release and is now identifying process failures to address in the next cycle. Planning for 10.1 is underway with a focus on fixing regressions from the hurried Auto DevOps launch.

bullets.text: Completed the GitLab 10.0 release including Auto DevOps.
Renamed the runner project.
Fixing bugs and regressions introduced during the final push for 10.0.
Developing a more structured deprecation process.
Manual and repetitive testing for Auto DevOps slows down iteration.
Background jobs stopping during deploys prevents work on the 7th.

content.tldr: While group issue boards and Auto DevOps were big wins, the 10.0 release was marred by poor coordination and late involvement of UX and frontend teams. The retrospective itself was criticized for lacking deep discussion and follow-up on action items.

bullets.text: The team successfully coordinated complex labels and milestones for group boards.
Shipped protected runners and variables despite low capacity.
RC1 was delayed due to large merge conflicts between branches.
The renaming of the runner project caused widespread 404 errors.
UX and frontend were brought into the Auto DevOps project too late.
Schedule separate calls to dig deeper into specific problems.
Focus on fixing one major product and one major engineering process per month.
Implement 'product discovery' to ship end-to-end iterations in one week.

content.tldr: The meeting was an internal technical retrospective and did not involve sales negotiations or budget discussions with prospects.

bullets.text: No external prospects were involved in this meeting.
No sales objections were discussed.
No financial budgets were discussed.
No sales follow-ups were generated.

content.tldr: Eric, as a new team member, is assigned responsibility for refining the retrospective process. The team discussed the need for better discipline in following through on improvements.

bullets.text: Eric joined the team and is on his second day.
Engineering feels they have backed off from leading the retrospective meeting.
The meeting feels like reading a script rather than a discussion.
UX decisions need to be respected more consistently.
Eric will bring discipline and slow, significant change to the process over time.
